frameworkProfile.title: Competence in psychological practice and research
frameworkProfile.status: Draft for the learning game and curriculum development; subject review is still required.
frameworkProfile.limitation: The domains are related. Unique ownership prevents duplicate recording; it does not establish psychometric independence. This model has not been validated as a measurement instrument.
frameworkProfile.careerNotice: These views connect professional activities to learning opportunities. They assess neither personal suitability nor eligibility to practise. Completing the game does not replace education, supervision or legally required qualifications.
frameworkProfile.opportunityNotice: Built modules show planned learning opportunities. Task levels describe the proposed work; personal competence is unassessed. Topic-dependent tasks still need an agreed topic and context.
frameworkProfile.gamePracticeNotice: Quiz and quest completion records practice in this game. It is not assessed evidence for module objectives or competence levels.
frameworkProfile.milestoneRule: Study milestones organise learning opportunities. Semesters, credits, buildings and completed quizzes do not establish a competence level.
frameworkProfile.futureCoverageRule: These links make future skills visible. They are not additional competence scales: a criterion may appear in several thematic views but is recorded only in its canonical location. The first twelve links draw on AIComp; the final two make further future-oriented questions explicit.
futureDesignTests: Does the objective remain useful if today’s AI tool is replaced?
Must students develop a question, alternative or justified decision themselves?
Is it clear where AI assists, where it is itself the subject of inquiry and which steps are undertaken or assessed independently without AI?
Does the task account for uncertainty, system effects and the perspectives of affected people?
Does feedback change subsequent action rather than merely award points?
Is the new learning component integrated into the existing workload and tied to a specific previous activity?

levels.label: I
levels.title: Reason with guidance
levels.description: Work on bounded tasks using supplied criteria and explain the reasoning.

levels.label: II
levels.title: Make independent decisions
levels.description: Select suitable methods for typical disciplinary tasks, compare alternatives and support the decision with evidence.

levels.label: III
levels.title: Address complex situations
levels.description: Develop an approach under uncertainty, new conditions or competing goals, examine its limits and take responsibility for decisions.

studyMilestones.title: Master: complex disciplinary and research tasks

futureLenses.title: Initiative and implementation
futureLenses.description: Turn an open practice problem into a justified project and organise the next steps independently.

futureLenses.title: System design
futureLenses.description: Design and test a research workflow with human and AI-assisted steps, keeping failures manageable.

futureLenses.title: Creative problem solving
futureLenses.description: Develop several personal approaches to an unresolved care or research question before consulting tool suggestions.

futureLenses.title: Critical digital competence
futureLenses.description: Examine a system’s technical suitability, evidential value and ethical acceptability using three distinct criteria.

futureLenses.title: Decision-making under uncertainty
futureLenses.description: Justify a bounded decision despite conflicting findings and state what new information would change it.

futureLenses.title: Reflect on self-efficacy
futureLenses.description: Compare personal confidence with concrete work experiences. Keep self-report separate from evidence of competence.

futureLenses.title: Critical thinking
futureLenses.description: Examine assumptions and alternatives in theories, measurement and analysis with justification. Human and generated claims face the same evidential standards; assessment uses the relevant criterion in each case.

futureLenses.title: Active control
futureLenses.description: Set personal goals, manage information load and decide when to calculate, decide or seek help personally in an AI-assisted project; adjust tools accordingly.

futureLenses.title: Self-determination
futureLenses.description: Justify using or declining AI through personal goals, protected interests and professional limits.

futureLenses.title: Ethical judgement
futureLenses.description: Address competing aims of individual support, fairness and privacy in a fictional AI system.

futureLenses.title: Cooperation
futureLenses.description: Allocate responsibility in an interdisciplinary team using AI so that handovers and human decisions remain traceable.

futureLenses.title: Communication
futureLenses.description: Explain an uncertain research finding and the role of AI to different participants; engage with differing views and clarify misunderstandings.

futureLenses.title: Systems thinking
futureLenses.description: Consider feedback between people, institutions and technical systems when planning change.

futureLenses.title: Learning amid technological change
futureLenses.description: Learn an unfamiliar tool through stable disciplinary criteria and address personal knowledge gaps.

aiAcrossCurriculum.title: Consider AI across every competence domain
aiAcrossCurriculum.principle: AI changes psychological questions, working practices and consequences. Disciplinary understanding, scientific scrutiny, professional action, collaboration and responsibility retain their own criteria. T1–T3 describe the technical part. All six domains can include tasks without AI, with AI or about AI.
aiAcrossCurriculum.assessmentNotice: This view organises learning opportunities. It does not establish attainment. AI use, tool access, source counts, credits and completed game activities are not competence evidence. A performance is assessed against the relevant canonical criterion; AI and future skills views add no further credit.
aiAcrossCurriculum.flowRule: The connections show common transitions within a disciplinary task, not a fixed learning sequence or an additional scale. Following a connection leads to the existing criterion. Each criterion keeps the same meaning throughout.

dimensions.title: Knowledge and understanding
dimensions.description: Connect psychological concepts, methods and findings with knowledge of AI and its conditions of use. A generated explanation still needs disciplinary justification.

dimensions.title: Capabilities and reasoned action
dimensions.description: Develop questions, investigate, decide, design and communicate through personal reasoning. Appropriate support depends on the learning objective and the specific step.

dimensions.title: Attitudes and self-regulation
dimensions.description: Show curiosity, reasoned scepticism, openness to counterevidence and willingness to revise through action. Self-reported confidence does not measure these attitudes.

dimensions.title: Values and responsibility
dimensions.description: Consider autonomy, integrity, fairness, wellbeing and social or environmental consequences in decisions. Assess reasoned deliberation, not a person’s private convictions.

domainRows.summary: AI may supply alternative explanations; trust in automation, anthropomorphism and changing learning or living conditions are also psychological subjects.
domainRows.learnerResponsibility: Students explain mechanisms themselves, distinguish competing models and consider development and social context. Plausible language does not replace a psychological model.
domainRows.evidenceFocus: P1 addresses the disciplinary explanation; P2 its context and transferability. The strength of a cited study remains under R4.

domainRows.summary: Research may investigate AI; AI can support searching, measurement and analysis. Generated claims, instruments and analyses require scientific scrutiny.
domainRows.learnerResponsibility: Students formulate a testable question, justify design and measurement, understand their analysis and examine sources, inferences and counterevidence. They state what the data cannot resolve.
domainRows.evidenceFocus: R1: investigation design; R2: measurement quality; R3: reproducible analysis; R4: strength of sources and claims. Evaluating AI output belongs here according to its subject, not automatically under T.

domainRows.summary: AI may offer case hypotheses, intervention ideas or design proposals. Its use also changes the conditions of psychological care, work and education.
domainRows.learnerResponsibility: Students clarify the task, integrate case information, examine alternatives and design changes with disciplinary justification. People remain responsible for decisions and their limits.
domainRows.evidenceFocus: H1 addresses the case-specific conclusion; H2 the need, proposed mechanisms and adaptation of change. Measurement quality remains R2, empirical effect evidence R4 and ethical acceptability V1.

domainRows.summary: AI can support drafting, translation and fictional dialogue practice. People must explain its use, establish shared understanding and organise responsibility together.
domainRows.learnerResponsibility: Students listen to people, respond to perspectives and relational tensions and make decisions understandable to those involved. A suitable chatbot response does not establish competence in human relationships.
domainRows.evidenceFocus: K1: clear presentation; K2: conversation and relationships; K3: coordination between people. Technical workflow interfaces are assessed under T3.

domainRows.summary: Technical understanding, purposeful operation and system design enable controlled use. Model mechanisms and technical failures can also be investigated without actively using AI.
domainRows.learnerResponsibility: Students explain data flows and limitations, translate tasks into suitable inputs, retain operating records and develop testable workflows with opportunities for human intervention.
domainRows.evidenceFocus: T1: functional understanding; T2: input, operation and technical records; T3: components, interfaces and functional tests. Disciplinary correctness remains with its disciplinary criterion, consequences with V1.

domainRows.summary: AI raises questions about protected interests, power, access and longer-term consequences. It also changes learning strategies, confidence and the allocation of personal reasoning.
domainRows.learnerResponsibility: Students weigh benefits, risks and values, limit delegation and may decline AI with justification. They check understanding through their own performance and adapt support and learning strategies.
domainRows.evidenceFocus: V1: ethical deliberation and defensible conduct; V2: reasoned self-regulation. Confidence in personal capabilities remains visibly self-reported; disciplinary performance is assessed separately.

flowEdges.label: From an explanation to a testable question and counterevidence
Use measurement and research evidence in a bounded case judgement
Align human handovers and technical interfaces
Connect functional testing with scientific scrutiny
Consider technical possibilities alongside consequences and protected interests
Revisit personal understanding and changing learning conditions
Build limits of responsibility into implementation

phases.title: Without AI: reason and demonstrate independently
phases.purpose: Develop personal knowledge, approaches and judgement, or observe them under known conditions.
phases.learnerAction: For example, first develop an explanation, hypothesis, case formulation or analysis decision independently; after supported practice, solve a new task unaided. Permitted non-AI aids are specified.
phases.assessmentUse: An announced section without AI can make independent work visible, such as a reasoned short answer, live analysis, transfer task or oral explanation. It does not replace disciplinary assessment criteria.

phases.title: With AI: support, check and decide
phases.purpose: Try support at an appropriate point and examine its influence on the result and personal reasoning.
phases.learnerAction: Formulate a personal task, scrutinise suggestions using disciplinary criteria and justify accepting, revising or rejecting them. Prepared outputs or a local simulation may replace live access.
phases.assessmentUse: Assess the reasoned use of support and the required disciplinary performance. Relevant outputs, human revisions and responsibilities need to be traceable.

phases.title: About AI: investigate mechanisms and consequences
phases.purpose: Study AI and human–AI interaction as technical, psychological, scientific or ethical subjects.
phases.learnerAction: For example, explain trust in automation, examine the measurement quality of an AI instrument or weigh distributional consequences. Sources, prepared outputs and fictional cases can support this without access to an AI system.
phases.assessmentUse: Choosing AI as the subject creates no separate AI assessment. Depending on the question, criteria such as P1, R2, R4, T1 or V1 apply; a single performance is not counted twice.

assessmentRules.text: Context labels on an objective indicate possible ways to work on it. The same objective may use a prepared output without personal AI access or an active tool. Several context labels imply neither several acquired competencies nor several compulsory assessments.
Permitted AI use is justified for the specific learning or assessment phase. A module may combine several phases. This design view does not declare any entire module AI-free or AI-mandatory.

Before assessed work, the task, criteria, permitted aids, evidence format and treatment of AI outputs must be clear. Binding assessment conditions remain the responsibility of the relevant teaching and assessment staff.

Independent reasoning is deliberately developed and, where needed, observed separately. A later transfer task without AI can provide different information from a supported product; both are recorded with their conditions.
Criteria remain the same across phases. Assessments refer to specific evidence and must not be multiplied by displaying it in AI, disciplinary or future skills views.
The proposal requires no paid AI access. Prepared outputs, simulations and equivalent disciplinary alternatives should be available; legitimate support needs are considered when conditions are set.
A model response, source counter or completed learning check does not establish competence. The game keeps planned opportunities, practice, self-report and actual assessed work distinct.

examples.title: Examine a persuasive explanation
examples.assessmentProposal: Explain a new prediction without AI; examine model comparison, evidence scrutiny and reasoned self-correction separately through P1.2, R4.2 and V2.3.

phases.activity: Independently outline two psychological models and their differing predictions.
phases.evidence: Personal model outline with a justified prediction.

phases.activity: Compare a prepared AI explanation with the outline and an accessible original finding; justify revisions.
phases.evidence: Annotated explanation with evidence and a justified correction.

phases.activity: Examine whether confident wording or an authority cue influenced personal judgement; derive a further check.
phases.evidence: Brief reflection tied to the actual reasoning process.

examples.title: AI suggestions in a fictional assessment case
examples.assessmentProposal: Separate measurement quality, case interpretation and ethical deliberation under R2.2, H1.2 and V1.2. An oral explanation without AI can make personal judgement more visible; it does not create a clinical qualification.

phases.activity: Independently justify measurement quality and an initial case hypothesis using supplied information.
phases.evidence: Separate notes on measurement quality and the case hypothesis.

phases.activity: Examine a prepared alternative AI case formulation and produce a justified personal version.
phases.evidence: Case formulation with accepted and rejected alternatives.

phases.activity: Weigh whether the proposed system should be used in the fictional setting and which interests require protection.
phases.evidence: Justified decision to use or decline the system.

examples.title: Develop a traceable research workflow
examples.assessmentProposal: Explain a new analysis decision independently. R3.1 addresses analytic reproducibility; T3.3 technical error handling; K3.2 a traceable handover for others. Practice data may be synthetic.

phases.activity: Independently develop a testable question and initial analysis steps from an open disciplinary problem.
phases.evidence: Justified question and personal analysis plan.

phases.activity: Try support for one selected step, retain changes in the analysis script and test the workflow with faulty inputs.
phases.evidence: Reproducible script and a separate functional test record.

phases.activity: Explain within the team where technical success still does not permit a scientifically justified conclusion.
phases.evidence: Traceable handover with unresolved checking decisions.

examples.title: Conversation between simulation and human encounter
examples.assessmentProposal: Observe another peer sequence without AI through K2.1 and K2.3. V2.3 concerns reasoned adaptation of learning. AI role-play alone does not establish competence in human relationships.

phases.activity: In an agreed peer exercise, clarify a concern through open questions and reflect back understanding.
phases.evidence: Observed conversational sequence and specific peer feedback.

phases.activity: Use a fictional conversation or prepared AI feedback to revise a personal formulation.
phases.evidence: Justified revision tied to the student’s actual wording.

phases.activity: Identify simulation limits and differences from a person’s response; derive a personal practice goal.
phases.evidence: Reflection on observed limits and the next practice step.

competencies.title: Explain psychological models
competencies.scope: Connect disciplinary concepts, mechanisms and findings.
competencies.boundary: Study quality belongs to R4; the quality of an accessible presentation belongs to K1.

criteria.title: Distinguish core concepts and mechanisms accurately.

opportunities.moduleTitle: Introduction: statistics, emotion, motivation, social psychology
opportunities.text: Distinguish emotion, mood and motivation through their disciplinary features, including attributions to AI.
opportunities.task: First classify three everyday situations independently using the introduced definitions. Then compare a prepared AI interpretation with your answer. Using a fictional chat example, explain why emotional wording alone does not establish experienced emotion and identify missing information.
opportunities.evidence: Personal concept classification with an annotated comparison and a justified boundary case.
opportunities.successCriteria: Classification uses defining features rather than everyday associations. Emotional expression is distinguished from claimed experience; an indeterminate distinction remains explicitly unresolved.
opportunities.openDecisions: The teaching team selects findings, computational depth and accessible response formats.

criteria.title: Compare models through their assumptions and predictions.

opportunities.moduleTitle: Introduction: methods, cognition, developmental, biological psychology
opportunities.text: Compare biological and cognitive accounts of the same phenomenon and delimit an AI analogy on disciplinary grounds.
opportunities.task: First independently contrast the levels of explanation and one testable prediction each for a memory or attention task. Then examine a prepared AI explanation that equates human learning with storing text. Use course concepts to identify the missing assumption about the human mechanism.
opportunities.evidence: Personal model sketch with a disciplinary annotation of the AI analogy.
opportunities.successCriteria: Neural description and functional explanation are connected without being equated. A shared term such as memory is insufficient to establish the same psychological mechanism.
opportunities.openDecisions: Responsible lecturers agree shared examples and the scope of biological detail.

opportunities.moduleTitle: Introduction to clinical psychology and psychopathology
opportunities.text: Compare categorical and dimensional approaches using a case.
opportunities.task: Apply two supplied models to the same fictional symptom pattern and identify their different informational contributions.
opportunities.evidence: Annotated model comparison.
opportunities.successCriteria: Classification and explanation of a mechanism are distinguished.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers select clinical topics, appropriate case depth and arrangements for distressing content.

opportunities.text: Compare two attention models through a critical condition and check an AI suggestion against them.
opportunities.task: First identify without AI a task variation for which the models predict different outcomes. Then compare a prepared AI suggestion for the same variation with your matrix. Accept, revise or reject it through the model assumptions, then justify a new variation independently.
opportunities.evidence: Personal prediction matrix, justified revision and independently explained transfer.
opportunities.successCriteria: Predictions and revisions follow from model assumptions and differ in a testable way. Confident wording in the AI suggestion does not replace this justification.
opportunities.openDecisions: The module lead selects the task and human comparison data.

opportunities.text: Compare structural and process models of personality.
opportunities.task: Explain which different questions two models address for the same behavioural example.
opportunities.evidence: Model comparison with predictions.
opportunities.successCriteria: Description of differences is distinguished from explanation of processes.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers select test materials and offer equivalent fictional examples for personal self-experience tasks.

opportunities.text: Compare competing theories within the selected specialisation.
opportunities.task: Contrast two developmental, clinical or social models taught in the seminar through assumptions and opposing predictions.
opportunities.evidence: Theory matrix with a critical example.
opportunities.successCriteria: Both models are represented fairly; the difference matters theoretically and empirically.
opportunities.openDecisions: The actual course must specify specialisation, models, articles and assessment format.

opportunities.text: Compare normative and descriptive accounts of decision-making.
opportunities.task: Explain a public-goods decision or framing effect using two suitable models.
opportunities.evidence: Model comparison with different predictions.
opportunities.successCriteria: Normative rationality and empirical explanation are distinguished; deviation is not automatically treated as an individual deficit.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers select the game or decision problem and credible human comparison findings.

opportunities.text: Compare models from the agreed examination reading orally.
opportunities.task: Explain two positions and their assumptions and identify a finding that could distinguish them.
opportunities.evidence: Oral model comparison in a practice session.
opportunities.successCriteria: The response remains substantively precise and answers the question actually asked.
opportunities.openDecisions: Examiners agree the actual reading, scope and applicable examination conditions.

criteria.title: Explain a psychological phenomenon using an appropriate model.

opportunities.moduleTitle: Introduction: statistics, emotion, motivation, social psychology
opportunities.text: Explain helping behaviour through an appropriate social psychological mechanism.
opportunities.task: Match a vignette to diffusion of responsibility or pluralistic ignorance and justify the choice using a situational feature.
opportunities.evidence: Annotated vignette response.
opportunities.successCriteria: The mechanism matches the decision stage described; the alternative is distinguished accurately.
opportunities.openDecisions: The teaching team selects findings, computational depth and accessible response formats.

opportunities.text: Connect a cognitive function with an appropriate neural explanation.
opportunities.task: Explain a selected finding at functional and network levels and mark the link between them.
opportunities.evidence: Labelled explanatory sketch.
opportunities.successCriteria: The explanation connects levels and avoids simple one-to-one localisation.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers determine the methods introduced and expected methodological detail.

opportunities.text: Explain a clinical course through connected biopsychosocial processes.
opportunities.task: Draw a process map with feedback loops for a fictional stress or illness vignette.
opportunities.evidence: Annotated process map.
opportunities.successCriteria: Connections are justified by mechanisms; biological findings are not treated as the sole cause.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers determine appropriate proximity to intervention practice and select clinical examples.

opportunities.text: Explain an illness course as a reciprocal interpersonal process.
opportunities.task: Create a process sketch of stress, response and feedback for a couple vignette.
opportunities.evidence: Dyadic process sketch.
opportunities.successCriteria: Both perspectives and feedback loops are included; one person is not broadly blamed as the cause.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers clarify role boundaries and offer a written alternative for distressing conversational situations.

opportunities.text: Explain a behavioural barrier using a suitable health model.
opportunities.task: Relate a fictional intention-behaviour gap to a model and identify a changeable process.
opportunities.evidence: Mechanism-based case analysis.
opportunities.successCriteria: The explanation is justified through the model and considers available resources.
opportunities.openDecisions: The module lead specifies target group, model and feedback scope.

opportunities.text: Connect levels of explanation for a contradictory finding.
opportunities.task: Develop an independent explanatory sketch for a selected conflict between cognitive, motivational, clinical or social findings.
opportunities.evidence: Explanatory sketch with marked assumptions.
opportunities.successCriteria: The explanation makes the conflict tractable and distinguishes supported connections from independent assumptions.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers select an appropriately difficult conflict; level III is a task design choice, not an automatic consequence of semester.

levelDescriptions.description: Explain a familiar phenomenon using supplied concepts.
Choose between competing models for a new example and justify the choice.
Connect levels of explanation when findings conflict and identify model limits.

aiIntegration.possibleRole: AI can generate competing explanations or counterexamples for a psychological phenomenon. Human judgements about AI are also objects of psychological explanation, including automation trust and anthropomorphism.
aiIntegration.learnerResponsibility: Students choose the theory, state its assumptions and explain the mechanisms themselves. They distinguish a persuasive analogy from a defensible disciplinary explanation.
aiIntegration.assessmentFocus: Assess conceptual accuracy, model comparison and explanatory power (P1). Evaluation of evidence for a generated claim belongs to R4.
aiIntegration.exampleTask: Explain why someone follows an incorrect AI recommendation. Compare two psychological models with a generated explanation and derive a distinguishable prediction for each model.

competencies.title: Understand person and context
competencies.scope: Account for development, individual differences and social, cultural and institutional conditions.
competencies.boundary: This competence explains how context matters. Normative questions of fairness belong to V1.

criteria.title: Describe contextual and developmental conditions and reciprocal influences relevant to a question.

opportunities.moduleTitle: Introduction: methods, cognition, developmental, biological psychology
opportunities.text: Identify developmental conditions in an age comparison.
opportunities.task: Identify age, cohort and learning opportunities that may matter in a cross-sectional study.
opportunities.evidence: Annotated comparison table.
opportunities.successCriteria: Conditions are distinguished; a group difference is not automatically interpreted as development.
opportunities.openDecisions: Responsible lecturers agree shared examples and the scope of biological detail.

criteria.title: Interpret differences between people and groups without unwarranted generalisation.

opportunities.moduleTitle: Elective seminar: topics in lifespan developmental psychology
opportunities.text: Interpret a developmental finding without blanket group attribution.
opportunities.task: Compare two studies on the seminar topic in terms of age, context and within-group differences.
opportunities.evidence: Annotated comparison of findings.
opportunities.successCriteria: Means are not treated as properties of every group member; the scope of the finding is stated.
opportunities.openDecisions: The seminar leader selects life stage, topic, readings and suitable evidence; this design requires those choices.

opportunities.text: Interpret individual differences and AI-generated personality attributions without determinism.
opportunities.task: First formulate a context-sensitive interpretation of an entirely fictional profile independently. Compare it with a prepared AI description that predicts fixed behaviour from a test score. Revise the attribution through variation and situation, then explain your interpretation for a new situation without AI.
opportunities.evidence: Personal profile interpretation with an annotated AI correction and justified change of situation.
opportunities.successCriteria: The revision considers variation and situation and avoids deterministic claims. Assessment concerns interpretation of individual differences; measurement validity is addressed separately under R2. No real personality profiles of learners are produced.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers select test materials and offer equivalent fictional examples for personal self-experience tasks.

criteria.title: Explain whether a psychological account transfers to a different life situation.

opportunities.text: Transfer an account of work demands to a different employment situation.
opportunities.task: Examine which assumptions of a work-demand model need adaptation for shift work or unemployment.
opportunities.evidence: Transfer analysis with contextual limits.
opportunities.successCriteria: The new context changes the explanation coherently; identical measures are not transferred without examination.
opportunities.openDecisions: The work setting and suitable technical examples are selected within the module.

opportunities.text: Transfer an explanation from the existing specialisation to a new context.
opportunities.task: Select a case actually taught in the seminar and examine which assumptions of a familiar model apply.
opportunities.evidence: Transfer map with required adaptations.
opportunities.successCriteria: The new situation is described substantively; assumptions that do not fit are identified.
opportunities.openDecisions: The specific module title, topics and assessment format are absent at slot level and must be added after selection.

opportunities.text: Examine a psychological explanation under substantially changed contextual conditions.
opportunities.task: Transfer a seminar finding to another life stage, service setting or work organisation and mark uncertain assumptions.
opportunities.evidence: Context comparison with transfer limits.
opportunities.successCriteria: The explanation is examined against the changed context; a universal effect is not presumed.
opportunities.openDecisions: The specialisation determines the target group and setting; ethical deliberation must use suitable supplied rules.

levelDescriptions.description: Recognise explicit contextual conditions in a vignette.
Distinguish individual, group and situation systematically in an explanation.
Account for changing contexts and intersecting disadvantages without treating categories as fixed explanations.

aiIntegration.possibleRole: AI can suggest changes to case contexts. Recommendation systems, digital relationships and algorithmic decisions also reshape the conditions psychology seeks to explain.
aiIntegration.learnerResponsibility: Students examine the social, cultural and developmental assumptions behind an account. They explain feedback between people, systems and institutions and avoid stereotyped generalisations.
aiIntegration.assessmentFocus: The focus is contextual explanation and transferability (P2). Normative judgements about disadvantage belong to V1.
aiIntegration.exampleTask: Compare two fictional students using the same AI learning aid under different linguistic and social conditions. Map possible feedback affecting behaviour, support and institutional decisions.

competencies.title: Design investigations
competencies.scope: Develop answerable questions and suitable research or evaluation designs.
competencies.boundary: Measurement instruments: R2. Data analysis: R3. Ethical acceptability: V1.

criteria.title: Derive a testable question or hypothesis from a problem.

opportunities.moduleTitle: Introduction: methods, cognition, developmental, biological psychology
opportunities.text: Derive a directional hypothesis from a cognitive explanation.
opportunities.task: Specify the comparison, expected direction and observable outcome for a supplied memory effect.
opportunities.evidence: Hypothesis with a justified prediction.
opportunities.successCriteria: The prediction is falsifiable and follows from the explanation.
opportunities.openDecisions: Responsible lecturers agree shared examples and the scope of biological detail.

opportunities.moduleTitle: Elective seminar: topics in lifespan developmental psychology
opportunities.text: Formulate an independently developed, researchable question about the developmental topic.
opportunities.task: Derive a question with an observable developmental outcome from an unresolved difference between seminar readings.
opportunities.evidence: Question memo with a theoretical rationale.
opportunities.successCriteria: The question goes beyond repeating an abstract and can be addressed through a bounded investigation.
opportunities.openDecisions: The seminar leader selects life stage, topic, readings and suitable evidence; this design requires those choices.

opportunities.moduleTitle: Elective seminar: social, economic, organisational, differential psych.
opportunities.text: Develop a psychological research question from a practical problem.
opportunities.task: Translate the seminar brief into a question whose outcome could distinguish between two explanations.
opportunities.evidence: Question paper with competing expectations.
opportunities.successCriteria: Concepts and observations are specified; a desired client outcome is not disguised as a hypothesis.
opportunities.openDecisions: The actual seminar must determine the topic, available evidence and prototype format.

opportunities.text: Independently delimit a manageable psychological literature question.
opportunities.task: Compare two possible questions and justify the selection through theoretical relevance and available literature.
opportunities.evidence: Question memo with a rejected alternative.
opportunities.successCriteria: The selected question allows an argumentative answer and fits the scope of a literature thesis.
opportunities.openDecisions: Supervisors must agree the question, search scope, permitted support, evidence format and any assessment adjustment.

opportunities.text: Develop an independent question to clarify the theoretical difference.
opportunities.task: First formulate a critical question without AI; optionally use questions from AI or a peer to refine it.
opportunities.evidence: Question with a justified revision.
opportunities.successCriteria: The question distinguishes the models and remains connected to the actual topic selected.
opportunities.openDecisions: The actual course must specify specialisation, models, articles and assessment format.

opportunities.text: Derive a new testable question from the unresolved conflict.
opportunities.task: Formulate an investigation whose possible result would change the independent explanation.
opportunities.evidence: Critical follow-up question with a falsification condition.
opportunities.successCriteria: The question allows an unwelcome outcome and limits its claim to the selected topic.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers select an appropriately difficult conflict; level III is a task design choice, not an automatic consequence of semester.

opportunities.text: Develop an independent research question from the comparison of talks.
opportunities.task: Formulate a question that could investigate an unresolved relationship between the two topics.
opportunities.evidence: Follow-up question with its anticipated contribution.
opportunities.successCriteria: The question is bounded and distinguishes a testable relationship from thematic similarity alone.
opportunities.openDecisions: The colloquium determines whether two talks can meaningfully be compared and which discussion format fits.

opportunities.text: Develop an independent master question from an unresolved disciplinary problem.
opportunities.task: Bring two possible questions and explain the theoretical or methodological uncertainty each would address.
opportunities.evidence: Question comparison with a justified selection.
opportunities.successCriteria: Selection identifies a substantive knowledge need and is not derived solely from available data.
opportunities.openDecisions: The chair and supervisor determine the topic, data access and proposal scope.

criteria.title: Match design, sampling and comparison conditions to the question.

opportunities.text: Plan an experiment suited to the research question.
opportunities.task: Before collection, prepare a plan specifying manipulation, comparison, sample and analytical decision.
opportunities.evidence: Dated study plan.
opportunities.successCriteria: Design choices are linked to the hypothesis; exploratory additions remain identifiable.
opportunities.openDecisions: Supervisors agree the project topic, data permissions, team contributions and which plan changes require justification.

opportunities.text: Plan a methodological alternative for the specialisation question.
opportunities.task: Design an alternative data collection method or comparison condition addressing the identified weakness.
opportunities.evidence: Alternative design with a justified trade-off.
opportunities.successCriteria: The alternative addresses the specific weakness and identifies its own limitations.
opportunities.openDecisions: The course selects the method and decides whether an AI component is substantively useful at all.

opportunities.text: Select an advanced method for a specific research question with a rationale.
opportunities.task: Compare the method taught in the course with a simpler alternative in terms of question, data and interpretative claims.
opportunities.evidence: Method decision with a rejected alternative.
opportunities.successCriteria: The more complex method is selected only when it addresses an identified knowledge need.
opportunities.openDecisions: The specific method, software and suitable failure cases must be specified after module selection.

opportunities.text: Develop a defensible investigation design for an independent research question.
opportunities.task: Compare at least two plausible designs and justify the selected approach under resource and knowledge constraints.
opportunities.evidence: Research plan with justified design decisions.
opportunities.successCriteria: The design addresses the independent question; decisive limitations and unanswerable questions remain visible.
opportunities.openDecisions: Supervisors determine topic, design, data use, permitted support and evidence. Level III describes demanding tasks and is not recorded as attained merely through submission.

criteria.title: Address confounds and limits to causal inference in the design.

opportunities.text: Identify an alternative explanation of a cognitive experiment.
opportunities.task: Examine whether a response-time difference could reflect task difficulty rather than the claimed process.
opportunities.evidence: Confound analysis with a proposed control.
opportunities.successCriteria: The proposal separates competing explanations rather than merely increasing the sample.
opportunities.openDecisions: The module lead selects the task and human comparison data.

opportunities.text: Respond to a critical design question using bounded causal reasoning.
opportunities.task: Address a question about confounding, comparison groups or selection and identify its implication for inference.
opportunities.evidence: Recorded response with a remaining design limit.
opportunities.successCriteria: The response addresses the objection substantively and does not claim causality unsupported by the design.
opportunities.openDecisions: The chair determines presentation time, discussion and whether a revision note is used as learning evidence.

levelDescriptions.description: Translate a supplied question into a simple investigation plan.
Choose between designs and justify sampling and control decisions.
Develop a feasible design for an open question under competing demands.

aiIntegration.possibleRole: AI can suggest design alternatives, possible confounds and simulated scenarios. Its effects on human behaviour can themselves become research questions.
aiIntegration.learnerResponsibility: Students formulate the question and justify the design, comparison and sample. Simulated data support planning and must not be represented as observations of real people.
aiIntegration.assessmentFocus: Assess whether the design can answer the question and address alternative explanations (R1). Ethical acceptability remains V1.
aiIntegration.exampleTask: Plan an investigation into whether AI feedback supports independent learning. Compare your own and supplied AI design proposals; distinguish immediate performance from later unaided transfer.

competencies.title: Measure psychological constructs
competencies.scope: Operationalise constructs and examine measurement quality.
competencies.boundary: Measurement quality is distinct from decisions about a person in H1 and statistical analysis in R3.

criteria.title: Translate a construct into observable indicators and suitable data collection methods.

opportunities.text: Translate a bounded construct into justified items.
opportunities.task: Create a content matrix and compare independent items with supplied AI items for coverage and double-barrelled wording.
opportunities.evidence: Content matrix with annotated item selection.
opportunities.successCriteria: Every selected item has a construct rationale; varied wording does not substitute for content coverage.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers specify available practice data, analytical scope and rights to test materials.

opportunities.text: Operationalise a biopsychological process for a specific question.
opportunities.task: Select behavioural and physiological indicators for a change hypothesis and specify when they are collected.
opportunities.evidence: Measurement plan linked to constructs.
opportunities.successCriteria: Indicators and timings fit the hypothesis; one marker is not equated with the whole construct.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers determine appropriate proximity to intervention practice and select clinical examples.

criteria.title: Judge reliability, validity and measurement error using appropriate evidence.

opportunities.text: Judge reliability and validity evidence separately.
opportunities.task: Examine a sample report containing a high alpha, factor solution and external criterion; justify one defensible and one unsupported use.
opportunities.evidence: Test review linked to the findings.
opportunities.successCriteria: High internal consistency is not treated as proof of unidimensionality or validity for a purpose.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers specify available practice data, analytical scope and rights to test materials.

opportunities.text: Judge what a neural measurement signal can support.
opportunities.task: Compare two introduced methods in terms of temporal or spatial resolution and indirect measurement.
opportunities.evidence: Method comparison for a specific question.
opportunities.successCriteria: Measurement limits are related to the question; visually compelling figures are not treated as evidence of accuracy.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers determine the methods introduced and expected methodological detail.

opportunities.text: Judge the quality of a selection method for a specific purpose.
opportunities.task: Compare a structured approach with a claimed AI selection method using supplied validation information.
opportunities.evidence: Method appraisal identifying missing evidence.
opportunities.successCriteria: The judgement relates to the selection purpose; high technical accuracy is not automatically treated as construct validity.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers select a recruitment or team case and the corresponding quality criteria.

opportunities.text: Judge the quality of a central measurement in the selected topic.
opportunities.task: Examine a measurement approach from an actual seminar article, such as a neural signal, prevention indicator or work characteristic.
opportunities.evidence: Measurement critique with a use-specific limit.
opportunities.successCriteria: The critique identifies the measured indicator and the claimed inference to the construct.
opportunities.openDecisions: The course selects the method and decides whether an AI component is substantively useful at all.

criteria.title: Examine norms, comparability and measurement invariance for the intended use.

opportunities.text: Examine whether test scores are comparable across groups.
opportunities.task: Interpret supplied invariance findings and norm information for an intended group comparison.
opportunities.evidence: Justified decision about the comparison.
opportunities.successCriteria: The decision identifies the comparability required and remaining measurement uncertainty.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers specify available practice data, analytical scope and rights to test materials.

opportunities.text: Examine the transferability of personality measurement to a new use.
opportunities.task: Compare questionnaire norms and validation information with a claimed AI inference from text.
opportunities.evidence: Justified boundary on use.
opportunities.successCriteria: The new data channel is not assumed to provide equivalent measurement; necessary comparability evidence is identified.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers select test materials and offer equivalent fictional examples for personal self-experience tasks.

opportunities.text: Examine measurement comparability as a condition for interpreting latent change.
opportunities.task: Interpret supplied longitudinal invariance findings before substantively interpreting an SEM change parameter.
opportunities.evidence: Justified interpretative boundary.
opportunities.successCriteria: Measurement change and construct change remain distinguishable; absent comparability is not ignored.
opportunities.openDecisions: The module lead selects data, SEM depth and a challenging sensitivity task feasible within the available time.

opportunities.text: Examine comparability between simulated and human decisions.
opportunities.task: Compare supplied model responses with human findings and identify validation needed before using them as a sample substitute.
opportunities.evidence: Comparability critique with validation requirements.
opportunities.successCriteria: Stable model responses are not interpreted as representativeness; systematic differences remain visible.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers select the game or decision problem and credible human comparison findings.

levelDescriptions.description: Distinguish construct, item, scale and measurement error in an example.
Choose an instrument for a question and examine its measurement properties.
Justify a measurement strategy for difficult populations or novel procedures and report remaining uncertainty.

aiIntegration.possibleRole: AI can suggest item variants or coding schemes. AI-derived behavioural indicators and automated ratings are possible new measurement methods whose quality must be established.
aiIntegration.learnerResponsibility: Students define the construct and judge operationalisation, measurement error and comparability. Plausible outputs are not automatically valid measurements.
aiIntegration.assessmentFocus: Evidence concerns measurement quality (R2), including possible changes across models or populations. A decision about a specific case belongs to H1.
aiIntegration.exampleTask: Design an evaluation of a fictional AI language-based measure of distress: which comparison data, reliability and validity evidence, and group comparisons would be needed?

competencies.title: Analyse data
competencies.scope: Prepare data transparently and analyse them using appropriate quantitative or qualitative methods.
competencies.boundary: Whether the resulting substantive claim is adequately supported is judged under R4.

criteria.title: Document data preparation and analysis reproducibly.

opportunities.text: Document data cleaning reproducibly.
opportunities.task: Import practice data, handle missing values explicitly and record every transformation in the script.
opportunities.evidence: Executable R script with a data log.
opportunities.successCriteria: A fresh run produces the same analysis table; exclusions and recoding are traceable.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers specify permitted packages and the technical assessment environment.

opportunities.text: Make the path from raw data to the experimental result reproducible.
opportunities.task: Generate analysis and figures in a clean script run and mark deviations from the plan.
opportunities.evidence: Executable analysis package with a deviation note.
opportunities.successCriteria: Results can be reproduced from authorised data; exclusions are not hidden.
opportunities.openDecisions: Supervisors agree the project topic, data permissions, team contributions and which plan changes require justification.

opportunities.text: Document a demanding methodological workflow traceably.
opportunities.task: Create a reproducible minimal example for course data or authorised sample data, including parameters and dependencies.
opportunities.evidence: Runnable minimal example with a method log.
opportunities.successCriteria: Another person can repeat the central step and locate discrepancies.
opportunities.openDecisions: The specific method, software and suitable failure cases must be specified after module selection.

opportunities.text: Document the investigation’s essential steps traceably.
opportunities.task: Create a controlled analysis or methods package with versions, decisions and justified deviations.
opportunities.evidence: Reproducible or methodologically traceable research package.
opportunities.successCriteria: An authorised reviewer can reconstruct central results; data protection limits are made explicit through abstracted examples.
opportunities.openDecisions: Supervisors determine topic, design, data use, permitted support and evidence. Level III describes demanding tasks and is not recorded as attained merely through submission.

criteria.title: Select analysis methods suited to the question, apply them correctly and examine their assumptions.

opportunities.text: Select a basic statistical analysis suited to the question.
opportunities.task: Justify the method for a group comparison and examine its relevant assumptions.
opportunities.evidence: Script section with a justified method choice.
opportunities.successCriteria: Measurement level and design fit the method; successful execution alone is not a justification.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers specify permitted packages and the technical assessment environment.

opportunities.text: Select a suitable model for a given data structure.
opportunities.task: Justify the model family, predictors and relevant diagnostics for a binary or nested outcome.
opportunities.evidence: Model specification with a diagnostic plan.
opportunities.successCriteria: Distribution and dependencies are considered; selection does not simply follow the smallest p value.
opportunities.openDecisions: The module lead determines which taught model families are used for the extended comparison.

opportunities.text: Specify a longitudinal model with an appropriate dependency structure.
opportunities.task: For repeated measures, justify time coding, fixed and random effects and examine a relevant model assumption.
opportunities.evidence: Model formula with a diagnostic extract.
opportunities.successCriteria: The model represents the data structure; within-person and between-person differences are not confused.
opportunities.openDecisions: The module lead selects data, SEM depth and a challenging sensitivity task feasible within the available time.

criteria.title: Interpret findings and analytic limitations with justification, including effect sizes and uncertainty or the defensibility of qualitative categories.

opportunities.moduleTitle: Introduction: statistics, emotion, motivation, social psychology
opportunities.text: Distinguish variation from uncertainty using a small dataset.
opportunities.task: Calculate a measure of variation and explain why a confidence interval does not describe all individual observations.
opportunities.evidence: Working and two interpretative sentences.
opportunities.successCriteria: Calculation and reference quantity are correct; variation, estimation uncertainty and probability are not conflated.
opportunities.openDecisions: The teaching team selects findings, computational depth and accessible response formats.

opportunities.text: Judge how robust a conclusion is to analytical decisions.
opportunities.task: Compare two defensible specifications and explain changes in effect and uncertainty.
opportunities.evidence: Sensitivity table with interpretation.
opportunities.successCriteria: Differences are linked to concrete model choices; a stable p value does not replace effect interpretation.
opportunities.openDecisions: The module lead determines which taught model families are used for the extended comparison.

opportunities.text: Bound a claim about change under differing model assumptions.
opportunities.task: Compare two defensible models for a supplied challenging dataset, for example with different time trends or missing-data treatment.
opportunities.evidence: Sensitivity report on change and uncertainty.
opportunities.successCriteria: The conclusion identifies supporting assumptions and findings that would alter it.
opportunities.openDecisions: The module lead selects data, SEM depth and a challenging sensitivity task feasible within the available time.

levelDescriptions.description: Follow a bounded analysis and explain its main quantities.
Analyse a dataset independently and check assumptions and sensitivity.
Compare complex models or analysis alternatives under uncertainty and defend a reproducible solution.

aiIntegration.possibleRole: AI can suggest analysis code, visualisations or initial qualitative categories. It may speed up analysis while making analytic decisions that go unnoticed.
aiIntegration.learnerResponsibility: Students select and explain the method, check assumptions and perform independent checks. They document data preparation, changes and uncertainty.
aiIntegration.assessmentFocus: Assess transparent, methodologically sound analysis and interpretation (R3). A tool’s operation record alone belongs to T2.3.
aiIntegration.exampleTask: Revise a supplied AI analysis draft for an open practice dataset. Justify the method and corrections; independently check a result or qualitative coding decision.

competencies.title: Evaluate claims and evidence
competencies.scope: Judge claims through sources, arguments and counterevidence.
competencies.boundary: This concerns the strength of sources and claims across cases, whether made by humans or AI. Diagnostic conclusions about a specific case belong to H1; AI evaluation receives no second score.

criteria.title: Check a source’s provenance, retrievability and actual claim.

opportunities.text: Trace the provenance of a central literature claim back to its original source.
opportunities.task: For an important passage, check the source location, actual claim and citation trail, including when a search tool suggested the source.
opportunities.evidence: Source verification note for the central passage.
opportunities.successCriteria: The original source and secondary account remain distinguishable; untraceable evidence is not cited as confirmed.
opportunities.openDecisions: Supervisors must agree the question, search scope, permitted support, evidence format and any assessment adjustment.

criteria.title: Check conclusions against methods, results and alternative explanations.

opportunities.moduleTitle: Introduction: statistics, emotion, motivation, social psychology
opportunities.text: Check an explanation of an emotion finding against the cited study.
opportunities.task: Mark an overstatement in a supplied AI explanation and replace it with a claim supported by the study extract.
opportunities.evidence: Correction with a source location.
opportunities.successCriteria: The correction considers sample and design; plausible wording is not treated as evidence.
opportunities.openDecisions: The teaching team selects findings, computational depth and accessible response formats.

opportunities.moduleTitle: Introduction to clinical psychology and psychopathology
opportunities.text: Check the evidential basis of a general treatment claim.
opportunities.task: Compare a supplied AI summary with a selected study extract about an intervention.
opportunities.evidence: Corrected claim with identified limitations.
opportunities.successCriteria: Population, comparison condition and outcome are considered; no individual treatment recommendation is inferred.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers select clinical topics, appropriate case depth and arrangements for distressing content.

opportunities.text: Examine a reverse-inference claim from activation to a psychological process.
opportunities.task: Revise a supplied popular or AI-generated interpretation of an activation figure.
opportunities.evidence: Corrected figure caption with a rationale.
opportunities.successCriteria: The correction identifies alternative processes and the quantity actually measured.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers determine the methods introduced and expected methodological detail.

opportunities.text: Judge a finding in the new area through its investigative approach.
opportunities.task: For a seminar article, create a short evidential chain from question through method to conclusion.
opportunities.evidence: Annotated evidential chain.
opportunities.successCriteria: Each inference is justified through the study; unfamiliarity is not covered by unverified summaries.
opportunities.openDecisions: The specific module title, topics and assessment format are absent at slot level and must be added after selection.

opportunities.text: Relate a central claim in the talk to the evidence presented.
opportunities.task: After the talk, record the claim, method and one inferential limit.
opportunities.evidence: Short finding note.
opportunities.successCriteria: The note distinguishes presented data from interpretation and outlook.
opportunities.openDecisions: The actual colloquium determines topic, available materials and discussion format.

opportunities.text: Examine an independent conclusion against a substantive objection.
opportunities.task: Answer an unprepared question about an alternative explanation and formulate a narrower conclusion if necessary.
opportunities.evidence: Discussion response with a justified refinement.
opportunities.successCriteria: The response distinguishes defending the result from defending every original formulation.
opportunities.openDecisions: The chair determines format and scope; confidential findings are shown only to an authorised audience.

opportunities.text: Examine a conclusion from the examination reading under a changed assumption.
opportunities.task: Respond to a practice question about population, measurement or design and bound the resulting inference.
opportunities.evidence: Response with a justified adaptation.
opportunities.successCriteria: The response uses the study’s approach and distinguishes established knowledge from an independent conjecture.
opportunities.openDecisions: Examiners agree the actual reading, scope and applicable examination conditions.

criteria.title: Combine findings into a reasoned judgement that accounts for uncertainty and conflicting evidence.

opportunities.moduleTitle: Elective seminar: topics in clinical and health psychology
opportunities.text: Synthesise differing findings on the seminar topic.
opportunities.task: Organise at least two selected studies by population, approach and result and formulate a bounded synthesis.
opportunities.evidence: Evidence matrix and synthesis paragraph.
opportunities.successCriteria: Contradictions are explained or left open; they are not removed by counting studies.
opportunities.openDecisions: The seminar leader decides the clinical focus, audience and appropriate proximity to practice.

opportunities.text: Produce an independent synthesis of psychological literature that retains unresolved contradictions.
opportunities.task: Create an evidence matrix and develop an argument containing counterevidence and a boundary on scope.
opportunities.evidence: Evidence matrix and argumentative chapter draft.
opportunities.successCriteria: Conclusions can be traced to sources; the synthesis follows the question rather than listing abstracts.
opportunities.openDecisions: Supervisors must agree the question, search scope, permitted support, evidence format and any assessment adjustment.

opportunities.text: Situate a contradictory finding within the theory comparison.
opportunities.task: Examine whether counterevidence primarily concerns model assumptions, measurement or scope.
opportunities.evidence: Counterevidence memo with remaining uncertainty.
opportunities.successCriteria: The interpretation is supported by the article and does not rescue the preferred model through unsupported assumptions.
opportunities.openDecisions: The actual course must specify specialisation, models, articles and assessment format.

opportunities.text: Bound a cross-disciplinary conclusion drawn from heterogeneous literature.
opportunities.task: Check whether two studies concern the same construct and outcome before interpreting them together.
opportunities.evidence: Comparative synthesis note.
opportunities.successCriteria: Non-comparable findings are not combined into an apparently definitive conclusion.
opportunities.openDecisions: The perspectives outlined are examples; the actual offering determines subject matter and collaboration.

opportunities.text: Justify a provisional synthesis under incomplete evidence.
opportunities.task: Examine the independent explanation against a deliberately sought opposing position and document remaining uncertainty.
opportunities.evidence: Synthesis with an opposing position and an open boundary.
opportunities.successCriteria: Counterevidence is considered substantively; missing studies are not replaced with plausible AI text.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers select an appropriately difficult conflict; level III is a task design choice, not an automatic consequence of semester.

opportunities.text: Synthesise two current findings from talks while retaining their differences.
opportunities.task: Compare two attended talks in terms of question, evidence and application and identify a defensible connection.
opportunities.evidence: Comparison note with a bounded synthesis.
opportunities.successCriteria: The connection is substantively justified; different constructs or populations are not overlooked.
opportunities.openDecisions: The colloquium determines whether two talks can meaningfully be compared and which discussion format fits.

opportunities.text: Integrate independent findings with existing evidence and alternative explanations.
opportunities.task: Write a discussion explicitly addressing counterevidence, an alternative explanation and an unresolved follow-up question.
opportunities.evidence: Discussion with an evidenced argument structure.
opportunities.successCriteria: The conclusion is bounded by design and results; unexpected findings are not smoothed away through wording.
opportunities.openDecisions: Supervisors determine topic, design, data use, permitted support and evidence. Level III describes demanding tasks and is not recorded as attained merely through submission.

levelDescriptions.description: Check a supplied claim against a retrievable source.
Compare sources critically and justify a conclusion.
Produce a defensible synthesis from conflicting, incomplete or generated information and state unresolved questions.

aiIntegration.possibleRole: AI can suggest search terms, lines of argument or counterpositions. Generated references and syntheses are themselves objects of scrutiny.
aiIntegration.learnerResponsibility: Students locate original evidence, check what it actually says and revise judgements when counterevidence emerges. They distinguish verifiability, plausibility and remaining uncertainty.
aiIntegration.assessmentFocus: Human and generated claims face the same evidential standards (R4). Explaining technical failure mechanisms belongs to T1; there is no second AI-evaluation score.
aiIntegration.exampleTask: Audit a supplied AI summary of a psychological controversy. Build a verifiable evidence chain, mark unsupported inferences and reach a judgement that accounts for conflicting findings.

competencies.title: Make psychological assessments
competencies.scope: Answer a specific assessment question using several sources of case information.
competencies.boundary: Test construction and measurement quality belong to R2, research evidence to R4 and professional relationships to K2. The same diagnostic case interpretation is not assessed there again. A learning case is not a clinical qualification.

criteria.title: Clarify and delimit the referral and assessment question.

opportunities.text: Distinguish a case assessment question from a suspected diagnosis.
opportunities.task: For an online vignette, formulate the open question before possible hypotheses.
opportunities.evidence: Structured case response.
opportunities.successCriteria: The question is bounded by the available information and does not presuppose a diagnosis.
opportunities.openDecisions: The module lead decides which feedback is automated and which is provided by qualified supervision.

opportunities.text: Translate an unclear assessment referral into answerable questions.
opportunities.task: Clarify purpose, parties, decision needs and assessment limits in a fictional referral.
opportunities.evidence: Referral clarification with outstanding questions.
opportunities.successCriteria: Questions fit the decision need and do not exceed the available information.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers determine case complexity, the role of conversation practice and lawfully usable materials.

criteria.title: Integrate information into a traceable case formulation with alternative hypotheses.

opportunities.moduleTitle: Introduction to clinical psychology and psychopathology
opportunities.text: Develop a provisional case hypothesis with alternatives under guidance.
opportunities.task: Connect stressors, protective factors and maintaining processes in a vignette; add an alternative explanation.
opportunities.evidence: Case sketch with hypotheses and missing information.
opportunities.successCriteria: The sketch remains provisional and marks assumptions; isolated symptoms do not establish a diagnosis.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers select clinical topics, appropriate case depth and arrangements for distressing content.

opportunities.text: Integrate conflicting assessment information into a checkable case formulation.
opportunities.task: Integrate interview, observation and test information; compare an independent formulation with a supplied automated summary.
opportunities.evidence: Case formulation with alternatives and evidence links.
opportunities.successCriteria: Contradictions remain visible; every hypothesis has supporting evidence and missing information.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers determine case complexity, the role of conversation practice and lawfully usable materials.

criteria.title: Justify a case judgement with uncertainty and further assessment needs.

opportunities.text: Formulate a provisional case judgement with further information needs.
opportunities.task: For a case task, justify the leading hypothesis, an alternative and a decisive next question.
opportunities.evidence: Judgement with an uncertainty note.
opportunities.successCriteria: Confidence matches the available information; the next question could genuinely distinguish the hypotheses.
opportunities.openDecisions: The module lead decides which feedback is automated and which is provided by qualified supervision.

opportunities.moduleTitle: Elective seminar: topics in clinical and health psychology
opportunities.text: Bound the scope of a case application of the seminar question.
opportunities.task: For a fictional case vignette, identify what the literature suggests and what individual information is missing.
opportunities.evidence: Bounded case application.
opportunities.successCriteria: Group findings are not converted directly into an individual diagnosis or treatment instruction.
opportunities.openDecisions: The seminar leader decides the clinical focus, audience and appropriate proximity to practice.

levelDescriptions.description: Organise information from a fictional case around a supplied question.
Develop a case formulation and consider alternative interpretations.
Integrate complex or conflicting case information into a bounded, justified judgement.

aiIntegration.possibleRole: AI can organise information or suggest assessment alternatives in fictional cases. Its recommendation may influence human judgement and introduce further bias.
aiIntegration.learnerResponsibility: Students justify the assessment question, integrate conflicting information and identify missing data and limits to their role. They examine recommendations against the case.
aiIntegration.assessmentFocus: Assess reasoned case interpretation, including uncertainty (H1). Measurement quality remains R2, relationships K2 and general study appraisal R4.
aiIntegration.exampleTask: Assess a fictional vignette independently, then with a supplied AI recommendation. Justify what you retain or reject and identify information that could change your judgement.

competencies.title: Design interventions and change
competencies.scope: Translate psychological goals into justified interventions or design proposals.
competencies.boundary: Effects are investigated through R1–R4. Relationships: K2. Ethical decisions: V1. No additional transfer score duplicates this work.

criteria.title: Derive concrete change goals from a justified need.

opportunities.text: Derive checkable change goals from an organisational problem.
opportunities.task: Translate a vague request for better teamwork into concrete goals that consider different parties.
opportunities.evidence: Goal agreement for the fictional brief.
opportunities.successCriteria: Goals describe changeable behaviour or conditions and make competing interests visible.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers select a recruitment or team case and the corresponding quality criteria.

opportunities.text: Derive a bounded prevention goal from a family risk.
opportunities.task: Formulate a mutually acceptable goal for the vignette and distinguish it from comprehensive treatment.
opportunities.evidence: Goal note identifying participants and scope.
opportunities.successCriteria: The goal includes resources and does not imply therapeutic responsibility for students.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers clarify role boundaries and offer a written alternative for distressing conversational situations.

criteria.title: Develop alternative interventions or novel design solutions, including for plausible future conditions, and explain their proposed mechanisms.

opportunities.text: Design two justified approaches to changing a maintaining process.
opportunities.task: Develop two different intervention points for the fictional vignette and compare their proposed mechanisms.
opportunities.evidence: Comparison of alternatives with proposed mechanisms.
opportunities.successCriteria: Approaches address identified processes; effectiveness and individual suitability are not asserted.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers determine appropriate proximity to intervention practice and select clinical examples.

opportunities.text: Develop alternative work designs from psychological mechanisms.
opportunities.task: Design an organisational and a technology-supported solution for a demanding work process.
opportunities.evidence: Two workflow sketches with proposed mechanisms.
opportunities.successCriteria: Both solutions change concrete conditions; technological automation is not automatically preferred.
opportunities.openDecisions: The work setting and suitable technical examples are selected within the module.

opportunities.moduleTitle: Elective seminar: social, economic, organisational, differential psych.
opportunities.text: Design different psychologically justified solutions for the brief.
opportunities.task: Design two variants, such as a message, team rule or decision situation, suited to the actual seminar topic.
opportunities.evidence: Two prototypes with a mechanism rationale.
opportunities.successCriteria: Variants differ in their proposed mechanism; visual variation alone is insufficient.
opportunities.openDecisions: The actual seminar must determine the topic, available evidence and prototype format.

opportunities.text: Develop an independent health psychology intervention with justified alternatives.
opportunities.task: Design an interpersonal and a digitally supported intervention for the same barrier and compare their mechanisms.
opportunities.evidence: Two justified intervention sketches.
opportunities.successCriteria: Variants address the identified process; technical novelty is not evidence of effectiveness.
opportunities.openDecisions: The module lead specifies target group, model and feedback scope.

opportunities.text: Design a new solution or change strategy from specialisation knowledge.
opportunities.task: Develop two independent variants of a cognitive learning activity, intervention component or application concept and justify the selection.
opportunities.evidence: Design with a mechanism and alternatives.
opportunities.successCriteria: Variants pursue an identified psychological purpose; selection and rejection are justified.
opportunities.openDecisions: The seminar leader must specify the disciplinary topic, simulation boundaries and technical support.

opportunities.text: Design a decision situation using alternative psychological mechanisms.
opportunities.task: Design two transparent variants of a fictional choice interface and justify the influence of defaults, information or framing.
opportunities.evidence: Two interface sketches with proposed mechanisms.
opportunities.successCriteria: Variants differ functionally and justify the expected effect; a revenue effect alone does not determine selection.
opportunities.openDecisions: Lecturers select the game or decision problem and credible human comparison findings.

opportunities.text: Develop a justified independent design from the actual seminar topic.
opportunities.task: Design a small explanatory, measurement or application concept and compare it with an independent alternative.
opportunities.evidence: Design with a comparison of alternatives.
opportunities.successCriteria: The disciplinary purpose and mechanism are traceable; the topic is not invented from the slot name.
opportunities.openDecisions: The actual seminar offering must be specified. For 505, the inherited module’s own six credits apply, rather than the generic slot’s four credits.

criteria.title: Adapt implementation to resources, feedback and changing conditions.

opportunities.text: Adapt an intervention to a target group’s resources and feedback.
opportunities.task: Revise the design after supplied feedback on access, time or burden.
opportunities.evidence: Revised design with a rationale for changes.
opportunities.successCriteria: The change addresses the specific barrier and preserves or revises the proposed mechanism.
opportunities.openDecisions: The module lead specifies target group, model and feedback scope.

opportunities.text: Adapt an intervention with a rationale under competing requirements.
opportunities.task: Revise an independent proposal after feedback on unequal access and limited resources.
opportunities.evidence: Adapted design with an unresolved trade-off.
opportunities.successCriteria: The adaptation addresses the feedback and documents which goals cannot be achieved simultaneously.
opportunities.openDecisions: The specialisation determines the target group and setting; ethical deliberation must use suitable supplied rules.

opportunities.text: Modify a psychological design in response to unexpected feedback.
opportunities.task: Revise a plasticity, intervention or application proposal after prepared counterevidence or an implementation barrier.
opportunities.evidence: Revised design compared with the starting point.
opportunities.successCriteria: The change responds to the disruption and explains which mechanisms are retained or abandoned.
opportunities.openDecisions: The lecturer selects the disruption and checks whether a digital tool fits the topic.

levelDescriptions.description: Explain a supplied measure and its goal for a fictional situation.
Compare alternatives for a bounded need and develop a feasible proposal.
Develop a justified solution under competing goals, address implementation barriers and take responsibility for adaptations.

aiIntegration.possibleRole: AI can draft variants of prevention, counselling or organisational interventions. AI-assisted interventions also change contact, access and the distribution of responsibility.
